etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English quik, quic, from Old English cwic (“alive”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwiku, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”), from *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”), *gʷeyh₃w- (“to live”).

Cognate with Dutch kwik, kwiek, German keck, Danish kvik (“quick, quick-witted”) and Danish kæk (“bold; spirited”), Swedish kvick; and (from Indo-European) with Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”), Latin vivus, Lithuanian gývas (“alive”), Latvian dzīvs (“alive”), Russian живо́й (živój), Polish żywy (“alive”), Welsh byw (“alive”), Irish beo (“alive”), biathaigh (“feed”), Northern Kurdish jîn (“to live”), jiyan (“life”), giyan (“soul”), can (“soul”), Sanskrit जीव (jīva, “living”), Albanian nxit (“to urge, stimulate”). Doublet of jiva.

definitions.definition: Moving with speed, rapidity or swiftness, or capable of doing so; rapid; fast.

quote.citation: 2017, Danna Staaf, Squid Empire, ForeEdge, →ISBN, page 87:
quote.text: The quickest and nimblest were probably the oxycones, throwing themselves through the water like discuses.

definitions.definition: Occurring in a short time; happening or done rapidly.

quote.citation: 2023 December 27, Zachary Small, “Video Games Let Them Choose a Role. Their Transgender Identities Flourished.”, in The New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: Veronica Ripley, 32, often speaks to friends about the role that video games played in her trans awakening: “I would try to explain it away, saying that I was playing the girl character because she had a smaller hitbox or quicker kill animations,” she said, referring to in-game advantages.

definitions.definition: Lively, fast-thinking, witty, intelligent.
Mentally agile, alert, perceptive.
(of people or tempers) Easily aroused to anger; quick-tempered.

quote.citation: 1549, Hugh Latimer, The Sixth Sermon Preached Before King Edward, April 6 1549:
quote.text: The bishop was somewhat quick with them, and signified that he was much offended.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Alive, living.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Timothy 4:1, column 2:
quote.text: I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Ieſus Chriſt, who ſhall iudge the quicke and the dead at his appearing, and his kingdome:

quote.citation: 1633, George Herbert, The Temple:
quote.text: Man is no star, but a quick coal / Of mortal fire.

quote.citation: 1874, James Thomson, The City of Dreadful Night, section X:
quote.text: The inmost oratory of my soul,Wherein thou ever dwellest quick or dead,Is black with grief eternal for thy sake.

definitions.definition: (archaic, of a foetus) At the stage where it can be felt to move in the uterus.

quote.citation: (Can we date this quote?) Section 316, Penal Code (Cap. 224, 2008 Ed.) (Singapore)
quote.text: Whoever does any act under such circumstances that if he thereby caused death he would be guilty of culpable homicide, and does by such act cause the death of a quick unborn child, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, and shall also be liable to fine.

definitions.definition: (now rare, archaic) Pregnant, especially at the stage where the foetus's movements can be felt; figuratively, alive with some emotion or feeling.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: she's quick; the child brags in her belly already: tis yours

quote.citation: 1941, Theodore Roethke, “Death Piece”, in Open House; republished in The Collected Poems of Theodore Roethke, 1975, →ISBN, page 4:
quote.text: Invention sleeps within a skullNo longer quick with light,The hive that hummed in every cellIs now sealed honey-tight.

quote.citation: 2012, Jerry White, London in the Eighteenth Century, Bodley Head, published 2017, page 385:
quote.text: When sentenced she sought to avoid hanging by declaring herself with child – ironically, given her favourite deception – but a ‘jury of Matrons’ found her not quick.

definitions.definition: (archaic, of water) Flowing, not stagnant.
(archaic) Burning, flammable, fiery.

quote.citation: 1922, E[ric] R[ücker] Eddison, The Worm Ouroboros‎[2], London: Jonathan Cape, page 18:
quote.text: And it seemed to me that the dream smote the roof above my bed, and the roof opened and disclosed the outer dark, and in the dark travelled a bearded star, and the night was quick with fiery signs.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Fresh; bracing; sharp; keen.

quote.citation: c. 1607–1608, William Shakeſpeare, The Late, And much admired Play, Called Pericles, Prince of Tyre. […], London: Imprinted at London for Henry Goſſon,  […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: […]  the ayre is quicke there, / And it perces and ſharpens the ſtomacke,

definitions.definition: (mining, of a vein of ore) productive; not "dead" or barren
Quickly, in a quick manner.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: If we consider how very quick the actions of the mind are performed.

definitions.definition: Answer quickly.

quote.citation: 2006, SpongeBob SquarePants, Whale of a Birthday:
quote.text: Quick, how do you spell 'Krabs'?

definitions.definition: Raw or sensitive flesh, especially that underneath finger and toe nails.
Plants used in making a quickset hedge

quote.citation: 1641, John Evelyn, diary entry September 1641:
quote.text: The works  […]  are curiously hedged with quick.

definitions.definition: The life; the mortal point; a vital part; a part susceptible to serious injury or keen feeling.

quote.citation: 1550, Hugh Latimer, Sermon Preached at Stamford, 9 October 1550:
quote.text: This test nippeth,  […]  this toucheth the quick.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: How feebly and unlike themselves they reason when they come to the quick of the difference!

quote.citation: 1941, Theodore Roethke, “Prognosis”, in Open House; republished in The Collected Poems of Theodore Roethke, 1975, →ISBN, page 5:
quote.text: O see the fate of him whose guard was lowered!—A single misstep and we leave the quick.

definitions.definition: (with "the", archaic) Synonym of living (“those who are alive”).
Quitchgrass.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto LXXXVIII:
quote.text: Wild bird, whose warble, liquid sweet, Rings Eden thro' the budded quicks

definitions.definition: (cricket) A fast bowler.
(transitive) To amalgamate surfaces prior to gilding or silvering by dipping them into a solution of mercury in nitric acid.
(transitive, archaic, poetic) To quicken.

quote.citation: 1917, Thomas Hardy, At the Word ‘Farewell’:
quote.text: I rose as if quicked by a spur I was bound to obey.
